semantic_correction.stem: A community health nurse is helping an employer plan worker safety education. What is a core purpose of effective safety training?

options.A: Teach workers to recognize and report hazards, understand controls, and use required safe work practices and protective measures.
options.B: Leave hazard recognition to supervisors so frontline workers do not need information about workplace risks or controls.
options.C: Provide safety training after an injury occurs rather than before exposure to a new task or workplace hazard.
options.D: Treat initial orientation as enough even when equipment, processes, materials, or assigned work later changes.

semantic_correction.rationale: OSHA identifies education and training as a core element of effective safety and health programs. Training should give workers awareness and understanding of workplace hazards, how to identify and report them, and how those hazards are controlled. OSHA also recommends training on work-practice and administrative controls, required personal protective equipment, and additional training when a change in facilities, equipment, processes, materials, work organization, or assigned tasks could introduce or increase hazards. Therefore option A reflects proactive injury prevention rather than waiting for an incident or restricting hazard knowledge to supervisors.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Recognize worker safety training as proactive education for hazard identification, reporting, controls, and safe work practices, including retraining when tasks or hazards change.
semantic_correction.source_organization: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Current OSHA Recommended Practices for Safety and Health Programs guidance accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Education and Training overview — workers need awareness of workplace hazards and how to identify, report, and control them. Action Item 1 — training includes hazard reporting and workplace controls. Action Item 4 — train workers on hazard identification, hierarchy of controls, work-practice/administrative controls, PPE; provide additional training when facilities, equipment, processes, materials, work organization, or tasks change
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: OSHA recommends proactive worker training in hazard recognition/reporting, hazard controls, safe work practices and PPE, with additional training when tasks or workplace hazards change.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed 'entirely/only' distractor cueing, shortened the correct answer, and preserved OSHA's proactive hazard-recognition, control, reporting, PPE, and retraining principles.

audit_findings_append.source_locator: Safety Management — Education and Training, especially Action Items 1 and 4
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — occupational injury prevention
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item directly tests preventive worker education without absolute distractor cues or supervisor-only responsibility.

option_audit.A: Correct. It reflects OSHA's core education-and-training goals for worker hazard recognition, reporting, controls, and safe practices.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. OSHA specifically trains workers, not just supervisors, to understand and report hazards.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Safety training is proactive and should occur before or when hazards and tasks change, not only after injury.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. OSHA recommends additional training when changed tasks, equipment, processes, materials, or organization can increase hazards.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone matches the complete OSHA purpose of preventive worker safety training.
cueing_check: All four options are safety-training strategies of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
